significance.sourceObservation:
The Lord's Prayer as Matthew records it ends, in some Bibles, with the words we say in church: for Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever, Amen. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus all carry it as part of verse 13 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition end the verse at "deliver us from the evil one" [S1, S2, S5].

Two things are worth separating carefully. The verse number is present in every edition; what differs is where the verse stops [C2]. And the editions are divided over the Greek: the closing words stand in the Byzantine and Textus Receptus editions and not in the Nestle text [C1].

There is also a translation question in the neighbourhood, and it is a different question. Whether the last petition asks deliverance "from the evil one" or "from evil" is a matter of rendering the same Greek, not of which Greek stands there. Both Berean editions footnote it, and the Majority Standard Bible keeps the two matters in separate notes [C3].
significance.interpretation:
Anyone who has prayed the Lord's Prayer in a Lutheran service has said these words, and they are printed in our hymnals. That is worth stating plainly, because a reader who finds the line footnoted in his Bible may wonder whether the church has been praying something it should not.

It has not, and the reason is not that the textual question comes out one way. As Larry Herzog Jr. puts it in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*, the doxology is the church's response to the Lord's Prayer in liturgical use [C4]. A congregation answering the prayer Christ taught with words of praise drawn from Scripture is doing something the church has always done, whether or not Matthew wrote those words at the end of verse 13.

What the difference does change is a question of description: whether the doxology is part of the text Matthew set down or the church's addition to it in worship. That is a real question, and it is not settled by comparing seven printed editions. A teacher can say what each edition prints, can point out that the words are in the hymnal either way, and should stop short of telling a class which the apostle wrote.

title: Why Some Bibles Have No Matthew 17:21

spans.text: But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.”
and this kind doth not go forth except in prayer and fasting.'
Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύεται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ.
Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύεται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ.

significance.sourceObservation:
In the Berean Standard Bible, Matthew 17 runs from verse 20 straight to verse 22. Verse 21 is not in the main text, and the same is true of the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition [S1, S2, S5]. Four of the seven editions compared here do print it: the Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation of 1898, the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine Greek text of 2018, and the Greek Textus Receptus compilation of Robert Adam Boyd [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The sentence reads, in MSB's wording, that this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.

Notice how the two publishers describe it. BSB's footnote at verse 20 says the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus include the verse; MSB's footnote at verse 21 says the critical text does not [S1, S3]. Those are two publishers' claims about groups of printed editions, and here they agree — which is not always the case in this book. Both also point the reader to Mark 9:29 [S1, S3].
significance.interpretation:
Follow that cross-reference and the picture settles. A closely similar saying stands at Mark 9:29 in all seven editions — though Mark 9:29 has a difference of its own, since BSB and Nestle print only "by prayer" while MSB, YLT, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd add "and fasting" [S1, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, C2]. So a reader whose Bible lacks Matthew 17:21 has not lost the saying about prayer, and a reader whose Bible has it has not gained something found nowhere else.

What that does *not* settle is how the difference arose. The two passages resembling each other is an observation; concluding that one was copied into the other, in either direction, is a historical claim needing evidence this comparison cannot supply. A teacher can say plainly what each edition prints, and can point to Mark 9. A teacher should not say that Matthew 17:21 was "removed," or that it was "added," on the strength of a comparison of printed Bibles.

title: The Gap Between the Little Ones and the Lost Sheep

spans.text: For the Son of Man came to save the lost.
for the Son of Man did come to save the lost.
Ἦλθεν γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός.
Ἦλθε γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός.

significance.sourceObservation:
Matthew 18:10 warns against despising one of these little ones. Matthew 18:12 asks what a man does when one sheep of a hundred goes astray. In the Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, those two verses sit side by side and there is no verse 11 [S1, S2, S5]. In the Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus, a sentence stands between them: that the Son of Man came to save the lost [S3, S4, S6, S7].

BSB also records the omitted sentence. BSB prints it in a footnote attached to verse 10, describing it as the reading of the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus; MSB, which has it in the text, footnotes that the critical text does not [S1, S3]. Both publishers point the reader to Luke 19:10 [S1, S3]. The disagreement is over a whole sentence in the Greek, not over how to translate one.
significance.interpretation:
This is a case where the argument of the passage survives the difference intact. The parable that follows *is* the statement about seeking the lost, told rather than asserted: the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one. Where verse 11 is printed, that point is stated first and then illustrated. Where it is not, the illustration carries it alone. A reader is not left in doubt about what Matthew 18 teaches concerning the lost, in either edition.

Nor is the sentence itself in question anywhere. Both publishers cite Luke 19:10, where the same claim about the Son of Man stands — and it is worth being exact here: that verse is present in all seven editions compared here, and nothing in this comparison touches it. What a teacher can responsibly say is that editions differ over whether Matthew states the point at this spot. What a teacher should not say is that anyone removed the gospel from Matthew, or that anyone inserted it. The comparison of printed editions shows the difference; it does not show which way the change ran, and this note does not claim to know.

significance.sourceObservation:
Matthew 23 is a series of woes against the scribes and Pharisees. Two of them are in question here, and the editions handle them in three different ways.

The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition carry one woe at verse 13 — that they shut the kingdom of heaven in men's faces — and have no verse 14 at all [C1].

The Majority Standard Bible and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text carry both woes, but in the order: defrauding widows at verse 13, shutting the kingdom at verse 14 [C2].

Young's Literal Translation and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus also carry both, in the opposite order: shutting the kingdom at 13, defrauding widows at 14 [C2].

And Boyd footnotes both verses to record that Stephanus' 1550 edition orders them the other way round from the two editions he collates it against [C3]. The Textus Receptus is not of one mind here either.
significance.interpretation:
So a reader comparing Bibles at this passage may find a verse missing, or present, or present in a different place — and all three impressions would be accurate reports of what different editions print.

What is not in question is the content of either woe. The charge of shutting the kingdom stands in all seven editions. The charge about widows' houses and long prayers stands in four of them here, and both publishers point out that it appears in Mark and Luke as well [C4]. Nothing Jesus is recorded as saying disappears from the New Testament on any of these arrangements.

What differs is how many woes Matthew lists at this point and in what sequence. That is a real question about Matthew's text and it is not answered by this comparison.

The useful thing for a teacher is the shape of the case rather than its outcome. Counting missing verses is a poor way to compare editions, because a verse can be absent in one, present in another, and present-but-elsewhere in a third. Only reading the passages side by side shows that.

<Υἱοῦ Θεοῦ>
Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ, υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ.
υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ
Ἀρχὴ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, υἱοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ.

significance.sourceObservation:
Mark opens: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. All seven editions compared here carry that phrase [C1]. But Nestle's 1904 Greek edition sets the last two words inside editorial markers — Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ⟨Υἱοῦ Θεοῦ⟩ — rather than printing them plainly [S5, C2].

The publishers explain why. Both Berean footnotes report that some modern critical editions omit the phrase while others keep it: on their account the Editio Critica Maior, the Nestle text and the Byzantine and Textus Receptus editions have it, while the SBL Greek New Testament and Westcott and Hort's edition do not [S1, S3, C3].

So this is not a case of old manuscripts against the traditional text. The traditional text and much of the critical tradition agree here, and the disagreement is among modern editors; the precise meaning of Nestle's markers has not been established from these chapter extracts. Note also that the difference is not visible in English style: every English edition on the list translates the phrase, and the question is whether the Greek carried it [C1].
significance.interpretation:
A bracket is not a deletion. Here the source includes the words and marks them. Without checking its editorial conventions, this comparison cannot say exactly what judgment the marks express.

What hangs on the phrase is less than it looks. That Jesus Christ is the Son of God is not a claim Mark makes only in his first sentence. It is what the voice from heaven says at the baptism, what the centurion says at the cross, and what the Gospel is arranged to demonstrate throughout. A reader whose edition brackets two words in verse 1 has lost nothing of Mark's confession.

Nor does the church's confession rest on this phrase. Lutherans confess with the whole church that the Son of God is true God, begotten of the Father from eternity, and true man born of the virgin Mary — the Nicene Creed's article on the Son, taken up in Augsburg Confession III [C5]. That confession is drawn from the whole witness of Scripture, and two words marked in Mark's first line neither establish it nor endanger it.

What a teacher should avoid is the reflex that a bracketed phrase about Christ's divine sonship is an attack on it. All seven editions here include the phrase; one marks it, and the Berean notes report that other editions omit it. Which of them is right is a question about manuscripts, and nothing in this comparison of seven printed editions decides it.

title: Mark 7:16 and a Sentence You Have Heard Before

spans.text: If anyone has ears to hear, let him hear.”
If any hath ears to hear — let him hear.'
Εἴ τις ἔχει ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω.
Εἴ τις ἔχει ὦτα ἀκούειν ἀκουέτω.

significance.sourceObservation:
After Jesus says that nothing entering a man from outside can defile him, some Bibles add a single line: if anyone has ears to hear, let him hear. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus all print it as verse 16 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not, and their text runs straight from verse 15 to verse 17 [S1, S2, S5].

Both Berean editions record the difference in a footnote — BSB at verse 15, attributing the line to the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus; MSB at verse 16, noting that the critical text lacks it [S1, S3]. Unlike some other places in this collection, neither publisher points you anywhere else. The difference is in the Greek: the editions that print the line and those that do not disagree about whether the sentence stood there, not about how to render it.
significance.interpretation:
The line is a summons to pay attention, and it is one Jesus uses more than once in the Gospels. Whether it stands here changes the pacing of the paragraph rather than its content: with it, the saying about defilement closes on a call to listen, and the disciples' private question in verse 17 follows a public challenge. Without it, verse 15 ends flatly and verse 17 does the same work by showing that the disciples had to ask.

There is not much more to be got from this one, and it is better to say so than to inflate it. No teaching rises or falls here. The honest summary is that a familiar refrain is printed in some editions at this spot and not in others, that both publishers tell you so, and that the reason lies in the underlying Greek copies rather than in anyone's translation policy. What a teacher should avoid is treating a short line as a test case for whether a Bible is trustworthy. A one-clause difference that changes no claim is exactly the kind of variation that gets recruited into arguments it cannot support.

title: The Refrain in Mark 9 That Some Bibles Print Three Times

spans.text: where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’
where their worm is not dying, and the fire is not being quenched.
ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ, καὶ τὸ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται.
ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ, καὶ τὸ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται.

significance.sourceObservation:
Start with the sentence every edition prints. At Mark 9:48, in all seven editions compared here, stands the warning about the worm that does not die and the fire that is not quenched [C2]. That is the fixed point. The question this note answers is how many times it appears before it.

In the Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus it appears three times: after the saying about the hand, at verse 44; after the saying about the foot, at verse 46; and again at verse 48 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. In the Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition it appears once only, at verse 48, and there is no verse 44 or 46 [S1, S2, S5]. Where 44 and 46 are printed, their wording is identical to 48 — the same Greek in the Greek editions, the same English in the English ones [C2]. BSB footnotes the difference at verse 43, MSB at verse 44, and both cite Isaiah 66:24 as the source of the language [S1, S3].
significance.interpretation:
Because the sentence is present either way, nothing about the warning itself is softened or strengthened by the difference. What changes is its shape. Printed three times, it works as a refrain: each amputation saying lands on the same terrible clause, and the repetition does the pressing. Printed once, the three sayings build and the clause falls at the end as a single closing blow. Preachers will have their preference. Neither is a different doctrine.

That is the whole of what can responsibly be said from this comparison. A teacher can show a class both arrangements and let them hear the difference in weight. A teacher cannot say, on this evidence, that scribes added the refrain for emphasis or that copyists dropped it as repetitive — those are historical claims about direction of change, and comparing seven printed editions cannot establish either. The identical wording at verse 48 is a fact; every story about how that came to be is a further claim needing further evidence, and this note does not offer one.

The same question arises again two verses later, at Mark 9:46.

title: Mark 9:46, and Why the Answer Is the Same Twice

spans.text: where ‘their worm never dies, and the fire is never quenched.’
where their worm is not dying, and the fire is not being quenched.
ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ, καὶ τὸ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται.
ὅπου ὁ σκώληξ αὐτῶν οὐ τελευτᾷ, καὶ τὸ πῦρ οὐ σβέννυται.

significance.sourceObservation:
Two verses after the question at Mark 9:44, the same thing happens again. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print, after the saying about the foot, the same line about the worm and the fire, numbered 46 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not, and run from verse 45 to verse 47 [S1, S2, S5]. BSB footnotes it at verse 45; MSB footnotes it at verse 46; both again cite Isaiah 66:24 [S1, S3].

The seven editions divide exactly as they did at verse 44, and no edition in this comparison prints one of the two without the other [C3]. The line is identical in wording to Mark 9:48, which every edition here prints [C2]. So, as at verse 44, no Bible on this list is short of the sentence; the editions differ over how many times it appears in the paragraph.
significance.interpretation:
Since this is the same difference as at verse 44, the same limits apply, and a reader is owed the same short answer rather than a longer one dressed up as new information. Where verses 44 and 46 are printed, the warning recurs after each of the first two sayings and again at the end. Where they are not, it comes once, at verse 47's conclusion. The sayings themselves — hand, foot, eye — stand in all seven editions [C4].

The one thing this second occurrence adds is a caution about counting. It would be easy, comparing Bibles quickly, to treat Mark 9:44 and 9:46 as two separate losses and to feel the weight double. They are one difference occurring twice, and the editions handle them together. Adding up missing verse numbers as though each were an independent subtraction is one of the commonest ways of getting this subject wrong, and this paragraph is a clean place to see why. What no one can say from this comparison is which arrangement stood in Mark first; that requires evidence of a kind these seven editions do not supply.

title: Mark 11:26 and the Warning That Is Still There

spans.text: But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your trespasses.”
and, if ye do not forgive, neither will your Father who is in the heavens forgive your trespasses.'
Εἰ δὲ ὑμεῖς οὐκ ἀφίετε, οὐδὲ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ἀφήσει τὰ παραπτώματα ὑμῶν.
Εἰ δὲ ὑμεῖς οὐκ ἀφίετε, οὐδὲ ὁ πατὴρ ὑμῶν ὁ ἐν τοῖς οὐρανοῖς ἀφήσει τὰ παραπτώματα ὑμῶν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Mark 11:25 tells you to forgive when you stand praying, so that your Father in heaven will forgive you. Some Bibles follow it with the negative half: if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print that as verse 26 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not, and run from verse 25 to verse 27 [S1, S2, S5].

Both Berean editions flag it. BSB's footnote sits at verse 25 and attributes the sentence to the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus; MSB's sits at verse 26 and says the critical text lacks it. Both send the reader to Matthew 6:15 [S1, S3]. The editions disagree about the Greek here, not about how to translate it — the two Greek editions in the comparison that print verse 26 and the one that does not are divided on whether the sentence stood in Mark [C1].
significance.interpretation:
Follow the cross-reference and the worry dissolves. Matthew 6:15 — but if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours — stands in all seven editions compared here [C2]. MSB records a wording difference and a literal rendering in its notes, but none of these seven editions omits the verse. The warning is not missing from anyone's New Testament. What differs is whether Mark repeats at 11:26 what Matthew records in the Sermon on the Mount.

Notice too that verse 25 already carries the substance. It ties your forgiving to your being forgiven; verse 26 states the same tie from the other side. A reader whose Bible stops at verse 25 has been told the thing the missing verse would tell him.

That is as far as the evidence reaches. A teacher can show both arrangements and point to Matthew 6. A teacher cannot say from this comparison that the sentence was carried into Mark from Matthew, or dropped out of Mark by accident — those are claims about which way a change ran, and seven printed editions cannot settle them.

title: Mark 15:28 and a Prophecy Quoted Twice

spans.text: So the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “And He was numbered with the transgressors.”
and the Writing was fulfilled that is saying, 'And with lawless ones he was numbered.'
Καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα, Καὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη.
Καὶ ἐπληρώθη ἡ γραφὴ ἡ λέγουσα, Καὶ μετὰ ἀνόμων ἐλογίσθη.

significance.sourceObservation:
Mark 15:27 has two robbers crucified with Jesus, one on each side. Some Bibles add a sentence: that the Scripture was fulfilled which says, *and He was numbered with the transgressors*. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print it as verse 28 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not [S1, S2, S5].

The Berean editions do not bury it. BSB footnotes it at verse 27 as the reading of the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus; MSB footnotes at verse 28 that the critical text lacks it; both point to Isaiah 53:12 and Luke 22:37 [S1, S3]. Two different kinds of footnote sit together at verse 27 in BSB, one about how to render "robbers" and one about this verse — worth not confusing, since only the second concerns what stood in the Greek [C4].
significance.interpretation:
The prophecy is not at stake. Luke 22:37 stands in all seven editions, and there Jesus himself quotes the same line about being numbered with the transgressors — in the Greek editions, the identical clause that Mark 15:28 carries [C2]. So the New Testament's claim that Isaiah's words were fulfilled in the crucifixion is untouched by this difference.

What changes is who makes it, and when. Where Mark 15:28 is printed, the narrator stops the account to say that the Scripture was fulfilled, at the moment the two robbers are named. Where it is not, Mark reports the scene and leaves the connection unmade, while Luke has already recorded Jesus making it in advance, on the night he was betrayed. Both are ways of telling a reader that this was foretold; one is comment, the other is prediction.

A teacher can say that much and should stop there. Which arrangement Mark wrote is a question about the history of the text, and comparing seven printed editions does not answer it.

significance.sourceObservation:
Mark 16:9–20 tells of the risen Christ appearing to Mary Magdalene, the commission to preach to all creation, and the ascension. Every edition compared here prints the whole passage [C1]. Six do not enclose the whole passage in such markers; English supplied-word brackets are a separate matter. Nestle's 1904 Greek edition prints it too, but sets the entire block inside editorial brackets, opening at verse 9 and running to the end of the chapter [C2].

So what the comparison actually shows is not a missing passage. It is a twelve-verse passage that one edition encloses in markers and six do not.

There is a second thing here, and it comes from the publishers rather than from the texts. The Berean Standard Bible and the Majority Standard Bible each carry a note at verse 8 saying that some manuscripts end the Gospel there, and that others carry instead a short ending — which the note then prints out [C3]. That short ending appears in no main text in this collection. The Berean notes report it, and Nestle’s source also preserves a Greek shorter ending as separately appended material, shown under “Edition’s separate alternatives.” Neither is part of the main-text passage compared here.
significance.interpretation:
A bracket is not a deletion. Here the source includes the passage and marks it. The precise meaning of Nestle’s markers has not been established from these chapter extracts, so the marks alone cannot tell us his editorial judgment.

What is at stake, if the passage were not Mark's own conclusion, is how the Gospel ends — with the women silent and afraid at verse 8, or with the appearances, the commission and the ascension. That is a real question about the shape of Mark's book, and it is a larger one than any single verse in this collection.

The evidence about which readers most often ask is set out by Larry Herzog Jr. in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*. The account below is reported from his book; manuscript readings, the critical apparatus and the cited patristic passages have not been independently checked for this note. On his account the witnesses he lists as lacking the longer ending — the Greek codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, together with Old Latin k, Sinaitic Syriac and Sahidic evidence — are independent witnesses from different regions rather than a single line of copying. He also cites two fathers who report on the copies in front of them: Eusebius of Caesarea, early in the fourth century, says the longer ending is absent from almost all the accurate copies and present only in some; Jerome, early in the fifth, says it is missing from almost all the Greek codices known to him [C6].

That is evidence, and it is worth weighing rather than counting. It is also not the whole of the case, and this note does not pretend to give the whole of it.

The resurrection, the commission and the ascension are also taught elsewhere in the New Testament. The resurrection appearances are recorded in Matthew, Luke, John and 1 Corinthians. The commission to preach to all nations is in Matthew and Luke. The ascension is in Luke and Acts. A reader whose edition brackets these verses has not lost the resurrection, the commission or the ascension.

Two cautions belong with that. The passage does contain sayings about signs — including the taking up of serpents — which have been pressed into dangerous practice; that is a question about how a text is used, not about which edition prints it, and all seven editions include those sayings, though their wording is not identical. And whether Mark wrote these verses is a historical question that comparing seven printed editions does not answer.

title: Luke 17:36 and a Verse the Received Text Does Not Agree On

spans.text: two men shall be in the field, the one shall be taken, and the other left.'
Δύο ἔσονται ἐν τῷ ἀγρῷ· ὁ εἷς παραληφθήσεται, καὶ ὁ ἕτερος ἀφεθήσεται.

significance.sourceObservation:
After the two women grinding grain, some Bibles add a matching line about two men in a field, one taken and one left. Only two of the seven editions compared here print it: Young's Literal Translation and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus compilation [S4, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, **the Majority Standard Bible and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text** all lack it [S1, S2, S3, S5, S6].

That last pairing is worth pausing on. Readers often picture two camps — old manuscripts on one side, the traditional text on the other — but here the Byzantine editions stand with the critical ones. Both Berean footnotes say so precisely: they attribute the verse to the Textus Receptus alone, not to the Byzantine text [S1, S3]. Both also point to Matthew 24:40, where a similar line appears in the Olivet discourse [C4].

Boyd's edition goes further and divides the Textus Receptus itself. His footnote records that of the three printed editions he collates, Stephanus' of 1550 does not have the verse, while Elzevir's and Scrivener's do [C2].
significance.interpretation:
So "the Textus Receptus reads" is, at this verse, an incomplete sentence. Three printed editions all called by that name do not agree, and a reader comparing a King James Bible with a Greek text labelled Textus Receptus may find them differing for that reason alone. An edition is a set of decisions by an editor, not a fixed thing a Bible either follows or departs from.

The saying itself is not in doubt as a saying of Jesus. Verse 35 and verse 37 stand in all seven editions [C3], and both publishers note that a similar line appears in Matthew's version of the discourse. What differs is whether Luke recorded the field alongside the mill.

A teacher can show the class the footnote in Boyd's edition and let the point make itself: even inside the tradition most associated with a single received text, editors have disagreed. What a teacher cannot do from this comparison is say which edition preserves what Luke wrote. That is a question about manuscripts, and none has been examined here.

significance.sourceObservation:
At Luke 22:43–44 an angel strengthens Jesus in Gethsemane and his sweat becomes like drops of blood. Unlike most passages in this collection, **every edition compared here prints both verses** — the Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus [C1]. They agree in including both verses, though their wording is not identical.

What you will find is a footnote. Both Berean editions carry the same one: that some manuscripts do not include these verses [C2]. That is a statement about handwritten copies, not about the printed editions on your screen, and it is the publishers' statement rather than one this note verifies or endorses.

The distinction matters. A comparison of editions can show you what publishers decided to print. It cannot show you what stands in manuscripts none of these editions reproduces.
significance.interpretation:
So the honest answer to "why is there a footnote here?" is that the publishers are telling you something their own printed text does not show: that the manuscript evidence for these two verses is, on their account, divided. They print the verses and flag the question. That is a reasonable thing for an edition to do, and noticing it is a useful piece of literacy.

What this note cannot do is tell you how that question comes out. Assessing which manuscripts contain the passage, and how old they are, requires a critical apparatus and the training to read it. Neither is in view here, and a note that summarised the footnote as though it were a finding would be passing off a publisher's claim as its own.

What can be said is narrower and still worth saying. The Gethsemane account does not stand or fall on these two verses: Luke's narrative of the prayer, the cup, and the arrest surrounds them and is present in all seven editions compared here. And a footnote in your Bible is not a warning label. It is an editor declining to keep something from you.

title: Luke 23:17 and the Custom That Explains Barabbas

spans.text: Now Pilate was obliged to release to the people one prisoner at the feast.
for it was necessary for him to release to them one at every feast,
Ἀνάγκην δὲ εἶχεν ἀπολύειν αὐτοῖς κατὰ ἑορτὴν ἕνα.
Ἀνάγκην δὲ εἶχεν ἀπολύειν αὐτοῖς κατὰ ἑορτὴν ἕνα.

significance.sourceObservation:
At Luke 23:16 Pilate says he will punish Jesus and release him. At 23:18 the crowd shouts for Barabbas instead. Between them, some Bibles print an explanation: that Pilate was obliged to release one prisoner to the people at the feast. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus have it as verse 17 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not [S1, S2, S5].

Both Berean editions footnote it, BSB at verse 16 and MSB at verse 17, and both point to Matthew 27:15 and Mark 15:6 [S1, S3]. MSB's footnote also gives a more literal rendering of the sentence it prints — a translation matter sitting in the same note as a textual one. Keep the two apart: how to render a verse and whether it stood in the Greek are different questions, and only the second is what divides these editions [C4].
significance.interpretation:
The sentence is an aside, not an event. It explains a custom rather than reporting an action, and its job is to tell a reader why a prisoner is suddenly on offer. Where it is absent, that job is done elsewhere: Mark 15:6 reports the same custom in all seven editions on this list [C2]. BSB and MSB add a note giving a literal rendering; neither note says the verse is absent. A reader working through Luke alone will meet the crowd's demand with less preparation; a reader with the four Gospels in hand is not missing anything.

The narrative does not stumble either way. Pilate's offer, the crowd's counter-demand, and Barabbas himself are all in the passage regardless.

What a teacher should resist is the temptation to make an explanatory aside carry weight it never had. Nothing about Pilate's conduct, the crowd's guilt, or the innocence Luke has him declare three times depends on whether verse 17 is printed. And whether Luke wrote the sentence or a later hand supplied it from the other Gospels is a historical question this comparison cannot decide, in either direction.

title: Only Begotten God, or Only Begotten Son: John 1:18

spans.text: No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is Himself God and is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
No one has ever yet seen God. The only begotten God, the One being in the bosom of the Father, He has made [Him] known.
No one has ever seen God, but the one and only Son, who is at the Father’s side, has made Him known.
God no one hath ever seen; the only begotten Son, who is on the bosom of the Father — he did declare.
Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν πώποτε· μονογενὴς Θεὸς ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ Πατρὸς, ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο.
Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακεν πώποτε· ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός, ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός, ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο.
Θεὸν οὐδεὶς ἑώρακε πώποτε· ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός, ὁ ὢν εἰς τὸν κόλπον τοῦ πατρός, ἐκεῖνος ἐξηγήσατο.

significance.sourceObservation:
John's prologue closes by saying that no one has ever seen God, and that the one at the Father's side has made him known. The editions differ over how that one is named.

Nestle's 1904 Greek edition reads μονογενὴς Θεός — *only begotten God*. Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus read ὁ μονογενὴς υἱός — *the only begotten Son* [C1]. The English editions follow suit: the Berean Standard Bible has "the one and only Son, who is Himself God," the Berean Literal Bible "the only begotten God," while the Majority Standard Bible and Young's Literal Translation read "Son" [C2].

Both Berean editions footnote the difference, and each keeps it separate from a second, purely translational note about rendering the Greek idiom "in the Father's bosom" [C3]. Those are two different questions and the editions are right to separate them: one is about which Greek word John wrote, the other about how to put a Greek phrase into English.

Notice which way this one runs. The critical edition here carries the higher title.
significance.interpretation:
That is worth dwelling on, because it cuts against what many readers expect. As Larry Herzog Jr. observes in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*, at this verse receiving the older reading means receiving a higher Christology rather than letting one go [C4]. A reader who has been told that modern editions dilute the deity of Christ will find, at John 1:18, an edition calling the Son *God* where the traditional text calls him *Son*.

Neither reading is thin. "Only begotten Son" is the language of John 3:16 and of the Nicene Creed. "Only begotten God" states the same Person's deity outright. The prologue has already said in verse 1 that the Word was God, and all seven editions include that statement [C5]; so whichever reading stands at verse 18, the chapter confesses the same thing about the same Person.

The church's confession does not rest on this word either. Lutherans confess with the whole church that the Son of God is true God, begotten of the Father from eternity, and true man born of the virgin Mary — the Nicene Creed's article on the Son, taken up in Augsburg Confession III [C6]. That confession is drawn from the whole witness of Scripture. It is not established by John 1:18 reading one way, and it would not be endangered by its reading the other.

Which word John wrote is a real question, and comparing seven printed editions does not answer it.

significance.sourceObservation:
John 5 describes the sick lying in the colonnades at Bethesda. Some Bibles continue: they were waiting for the moving of the water, because an angel came down at times and stirred the pool, and the first one in was healed. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print all of that [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible and the Berean Literal Bible print none of it, ending verse 3 with the list of the sick and going straight to verse 5 [S1, S2].

Nestle's 1904 Greek edition does something different again: it prints the material but encloses it in editorial markers, opening partway through verse 3 and closing at the end of verse 4 [S5, C3]. The material is present and marked; the markers’ precise editorial meaning is not established by these chapter extracts.

Two points of precision. First, the difference does not start at verse 4; it starts inside verse 3, with the clause about waiting for the water to move, and BSB's own footnote says so [S1]. Second, what divides the editions here is the Greek, not English style [C1].
significance.interpretation:
What the passage loses or gains is an explanation. Without it, John reports a crowd of sick people by a pool, and the man Jesus meets says he has no one to put him in the water when it is stirred — so the custom is still visible in verse 7, in every edition [C4]. With it, the reason for the stirring is supplied, and attributed to an angel.

So the healing narrative stands either way, and so does the detail that the sick were waiting for the water to move. What differs is whether John's Gospel explains the phenomenon or leaves it as something everyone at the pool took for granted.

That distinction is worth keeping clear, because this passage sometimes gets discussed as though a miracle were at stake. It is not. Jesus heals the man by his word, with no reference to the pool at all, and all seven editions report that healing, though their wording is not identical. The disputed material concerns a popular belief about the water, not the miracle John actually reports. What no one can determine from this comparison is whether the explanation stood in John's own text; that requires evidence of a kind seven printed editions do not supply.

significance.sourceObservation:
The account of the woman brought to Jesus by the scribes and Pharisees runs from John 7:53 to 8:11. Every edition compared here prints it in full [C1]. Six do not enclose the whole passage in such markers; English supplied-word brackets are a separate matter. Nestle's 1904 Greek edition prints it and encloses the whole passage in editorial brackets [C2].

So the comparison shows no missing text. What it shows is that one editor marked twelve verses and six did not.

Something else is visible if you open the footnotes, and it is unusual. Within these twelve verses the publishers record a remarkable number of small differences — the Majority Standard Bible has twelve textual notes and one rendering note, while the Berean Standard Bible has three textual notes and one rendering note, naming a range of printed editions that read differently at one point or another [C3]. These seventeen Berean notes concern the wording and its rendering, rather than the inclusion of the whole passage. The notes can overlap in what they discuss; their number is not a count of independent variants.
significance.interpretation:
That density is the most informative thing here, and it is worth understanding rather than counting.

The notes show that the publishers report several wording differences here. Note density also reflects publisher practice, so it cannot by itself measure how settled a textual tradition is. The scale of the variation is not itself an argument about whether John wrote the passage — that is a separate question, and the comparison of seven printed editions does not answer it. The differences can be examined individually without inferring that the rest of John has none.

The manuscript evidence is set out by Larry Herzog Jr. in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*. The account below is reported from his book; manuscript readings and a critical apparatus have not been independently checked for this note. On his account the two earliest substantial papyri of John, P66 and P75, do not contain the passage — P66 running unbroken from John 7:52 to 8:12 — and the two great fourth-century uncials, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, both move directly from 7:52 to 8:12 [C7].

What is not in doubt is what the passage says. Jesus does not condemn the woman; he tells her to go and sin no more. All seven include both statements, though their wording differs. MSB’s notes at 8:11 discuss the speech introduction and “Now go.” Lutherans confess that law and gospel are to be distinguished and both rightly preached — the law convicting, the gospel forgiving — as the Formula of Concord sets out in its article on law and gospel [C8]; whichever way the textual question falls, that distinction is taught throughout Scripture and does not stand or fall with this narrative.

A teacher can say that all seven editions here print the passage, that one encloses it in markers, and that its notes report several wording differences, and that where it stood in John — or whether it stood in John — is a question requiring evidence this comparison does not supply. What a teacher should avoid is treating the bracket as a verdict, in either direction, or treating a reader's attachment to the passage as if it settled anything.

title: Why Some Bibles Skip From Acts 8:36 to Acts 8:38

spans.text: [And Philip said, 'If thou dost believe out of all the heart, it is lawful;' and he answering said, 'I believe Jesus Christ to be the Son of God;']
Εἶπε δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος, Εἰ πιστεύεις ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, ἔξεστιν. Ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ εἶπε, Πιστεύω τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Read Acts 8 in the Berean Standard Bible and you go straight from verse 36 to verse 38. Verse 37 is not there. The same is true in the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine Greek text of 2018 [S1, S2, S3, S5, S6]. Two of the seven editions compared here do print the sentence: the Greek Textus Receptus compilation of Robert Adam Boyd (2022), and Young's Literal Translation of 1898, which sets it inside square brackets [S4, S7]. "Textus Receptus" names the family of printed Greek New Testaments that began with Erasmus in 1516 and stood behind the King James Version [C7].

The difference lies in the Greek, not in English style: Boyd's edition and Robinson–Pierpont disagree about whether the sentence is there at all [S6, S7]. Nothing is hidden, though. BSB and MSB each attach a footnote at verse 36 reporting the Textus Receptus reading and printing it out [S1, S3]. In BSB and MSB, the main text skips verse number 37, while a publisher note at verse 36 prints the TR reading.
significance.interpretation:
The effect on the story is real but contained. With or without verse 37, Acts 8 says that Philip preached Jesus to the man reading Isaiah 53, that the man saw water and asked what was stopping him from being baptized, that Philip baptized him, and that he went away rejoicing (vv. 35–39) [S1]. Where the exchange is printed, the narrative pauses for a stated condition and a stated confession. Where it is not, the request and the rejoicing carry that weight without a quoted creed.

The verse is often recruited into arguments about who may be baptized; it is the one the Baptist tradition has cited for centuries against infant baptism. It cannot settle that question in either direction. The man in the chariot is an adult hearing the gospel from Philip, and the passage says nothing about anyone else. As Larry Herzog Jr. argues in *Ad Fontes, Volume One*, the Lutheran case for infant baptism rests on Christ's command in Matthew 28:19, on the inclusion of children in the covenant, on the household baptisms of Acts 16:15 and 16:33, on Colossians 2:11–12, and on Christian baptismal practice attested from Justin Martyr forward — a case independent of any one verse. On his account the absence of Acts 8:37 adds no ammunition to the Lutheran position; it removes a verse from the credo-baptist arsenal [C6].

title: Acts 15:34 and What Happened to Silas

spans.text: and it seemed good to Silas to remain there still.
Ἔδοξε δὲ τῷ Σίλᾳ ἐπιμεῖναι αὐτοῦ.

significance.sourceObservation:
Acts 15:33 has Judas and Silas sent off in peace from Antioch. Some Bibles then add a line saying that Silas decided to remain there. Only two of the seven editions compared here print it: Young's Literal Translation and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus [S4, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition, the Majority Standard Bible and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text all lack it [S1, S2, S3, S5, S6].

As at Luke 17:36, the Byzantine editions omit alongside the critical ones, and both Berean footnotes are careful about it: they attribute the sentence to the Textus Receptus, not to the Byzantine text [S1, S3]. MSB's footnote also carries a separate matter — a wording difference at verse 33 itself, where the two editions read "to the apostles" and "to those who had sent them" [C4]. The wording difference at verse 33 and the presence of verse 34 are separate textual matters; the latter concerns whether a whole sentence stood in Luke's account.
significance.interpretation:
The sentence answers a question the chapter otherwise leaves hanging. Verse 33 sends Silas away; verse 40 has Paul choosing Silas to go with him [C3]. A reader working straight through wonders when Silas came back. Where verse 34 is printed, it explains that he stayed. Where it is not, the account simply moves on, and the reader is left to assume he returned or never left.

That is a real difference in reading experience, and it is worth saying plainly rather than smoothing over. It is also the kind of gap narratives often leave. Luke does not say when Barnabas and Mark reached Cyprus either, and no one thinks something is missing.

What cannot be settled here is whether Luke wrote the explanation or a later hand supplied it. Both are conceivable and the comparison of seven printed editions decides neither. A teacher can point out the tension between verse 33 and verse 40, note that some editions resolve it and some do not, and leave the historical question open — which is where the evidence actually leaves it.

significance.sourceObservation:
Tertullus is prosecuting Paul before Felix. In some Bibles the speech runs longer: after saying they seized Paul, it adds that they would have judged him by their own law, that the commander Lysias took him from their hands by force, and that Lysias ordered the accusers to come before Felix. Young's Literal Translation and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus carry all of that [S4, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text do not [S1, S2, S3, S5, S6] — another place where the Byzantine editions omit alongside the critical ones.

The verse numbers describe this badly, and it is worth saying why. The extra material does not fill a missing verse 7. It begins partway through verse 6, runs through verse 7, and ends partway through verse 8 [C2]. BSB's footnote sets it out in exactly that shape [S1]. Editions that lack it therefore have a shorter verse 6 and a shorter verse 8 as well as no verse 7.
significance.interpretation:
What the longer form adds is Tertullus' account of how Paul came to be in Roman custody, with a complaint about Lysias' intervention. In the shorter form, Tertullus says they seized Paul and moves straight to inviting Felix to examine him.

The charge against Paul is unchanged either way, and so is Felix's response. What the longer form supplies is a grievance about jurisdiction — the claim that the Jewish authorities would have dealt with the matter themselves had the commander not intervened. A reader of the shorter text learns of Lysias' intervention anyway, from the surrounding narrative rather than from Tertullus' mouth.

This passage also belongs to something larger. Acts survives in an ancient family of manuscripts whose text runs roughly ten percent longer than what the modern critical editions print — the **Western text** of Acts, described at length in *Ad Fontes – Volume One* by Larry Herzog Jr. [C6]. Longer readings of this kind are its characteristic feature, and that is a claim about a whole textual tradition rather than about this verse alone.

The other lesson here is about reading. Verse numbers are a finding aid added in 1551, more than a millennium after the text they organise [C4], and differences between editions do not politely arrange themselves inside their boundaries. When a footnote says a verse is missing, it is worth checking whether the neighbouring verses are also shorter. Here they are. What this comparison cannot tell you is which form Luke wrote, and nothing in these seven editions settles it.

title: Acts 28:29 and the Reported Reaction

spans.text: And when he had said these things, the Jews went away, disputing sharply among themselves.
and he having said these things, the Jews went away, having much disputation among themselves;
Καὶ ταῦτα αὐτοῦ εἰπόντος, ἀπῆλθον οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι, πολλὴν ἔχοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς συζήτησιν.
Καὶ ταῦτα αὐτοῦ εἰπόντος, ἀπῆλθον οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι, πολλὴν ἔχοντες ἐν ἑαυτοῖς συζήτησιν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul's last recorded words to the Jewish leaders in Rome are at Acts 28:28: God's salvation has been sent to the Gentiles, and they will listen. Some Bibles then report the reaction — that when he had said this, the Jews went away, disputing sharply among themselves — before the account moves to Paul's two years in his own rented house. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print that as verse 29 [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not, and go from verse 28 to verse 30 [S1, S2, S5].

BSB footnotes it at verse 28 as the reading of the Byzantine text and the Textus Receptus; MSB footnotes at verse 29 that the critical text lacks it [S1, S3]. Neither publisher offers a cross-reference. That is unusual: at comparable places in this collection both send the reader somewhere else in the New Testament where the disputed words also stand, and here neither does [C3].
significance.interpretation:
That makes this the rarer case, and it deserves a straighter answer than the usual one. Elsewhere a reader can be told that the words in question stand somewhere else in every Bible on the list. Here neither publisher offers such a pointer. If the sentence was Luke's, an edition without it loses this reported reaction; if it was not, an edition with it carries one Luke did not write. Something genuinely turns on the question, even though the something is small.

What it is: a closing note on how Paul's declaration landed. With verse 29, Acts records the Jewish leaders leaving in sharp disagreement, and the argument continues off the page. Without it, verse 28 ends on Paul's statement and the narrative moves straight to two years of open preaching, so the last thing shown is not the reaction but Paul's continued welcome of all comers.

Neither arrangement changes what Acts reports about the mission to the Gentiles, which is stated in verse 28 in all seven editions [C2]. But a teacher should not tell a class that nothing is at stake here, because the honest position is that a detail either was or was not part of Luke's account, and this comparison does not establish which.

title: One Letter in Romans 5:1: Have Peace, or Let Us Have Peace

spans.text: Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Having been declared righteous, then, by faith, we have peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
Δικαιωθέντες οὖν ἐκ πίστεως εἰρήνην ἔχωμεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ,
Δικαιωθέντες οὖν ἐκ πίστεως, εἰρήνην ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν θεὸν διὰ τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ,
Δικαιωθέντες οὖν ἐκ πίστεως, εἰρήνην ἔχομεν πρὸς τὸν Θεὸν διὰ τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ,

significance.sourceObservation:
Compare the four English editions in this collection at Romans 5:1 and you will find nothing to compare. All of them say that, having been justified by faith, *we have peace with God* [C2]. Compare the Greek editions and they differ — by one letter. Nestle's 1904 text reads ἔχωμεν; Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus read ἔχομεν [C1].

Omega for omicron changes the mood of the verb. ἔχομεν is a statement: we have peace. ἔχωμεν is a summons: let us have peace. The printed forms differ by that vowel. This comparison does not establish how the difference arose.

Both Berean editions tell you about it. Each translates the statement and footnotes the summons as "Or let us have" [C3]. That is a good instance of a general point: a difference in the Greek can be invisible in every English translation on your shelf and still be there. Among these four English editions, the Berean footnotes disclose the alternative; the difference is also visible in the Greek comparison.
significance.interpretation:
The two readings pull in different directions, and it is worth being exact about how far.

Read as a statement, the verse declares a result: justification by faith has been granted, and peace with God follows from it. Read as a summons, it exhorts the justified to lay hold of a peace they have been given. Neither reading makes peace something we achieve. Both stand on the same clause — *having been justified by faith* — which is a completed action in either case, and neither reading makes that justification depend on what the hearer then does.

That last point is what a teacher most needs to make. Someone who learns that the Greek may read "let us have peace" can conclude too quickly that Paul is making peace with God conditional on our effort. He is not, on either reading: the participle has already settled how the justified came to be justified.

Which mood Paul wrote is a genuine question on which editors differ, and the comparison of these seven editions does not answer it. What can be said is that every English edition here translates the statement, that both Berean editions disclose the alternative, and that the doctrine of justification by faith is not what is at stake between them. Lutherans confess that we receive forgiveness and are justified before God by faith for Christ's sake, not for our own works — Augsburg Confession IV — and that confession stands whichever mood Paul wrote [C6].

title: Romans 16:24 and a Blessing Given Twice

spans.text: May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ [be] with you all. Amen.
Ἡ χάρις τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.
Ἡ χάρις τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ μετὰ πάντων ὑμῶν. Ἀμήν.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul blesses the Roman church at 16:20 — the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you — and then returns to greetings from Gaius, Erastus and Quartus. In some Bibles a second, nearly identical blessing follows at verse 24. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus print it [S3, S4, S6, S7]. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's 1904 Greek edition do not [S1, S2, S5]. The two are close but not identical: verse 24 adds "all." In Robinson–Pierpont it also adds an Amen; Boyd's text already has an Amen at verse 20 [C2].

Here the usual shorthand breaks down, and the publishers are the ones who say so. BSB's footnote attributes the verse to "SBL, BYZ, and TR"; MSB's to "SBL, MT, and TR," adding that other critical editions omit it [S1, S3]. SBL is itself a modern critical edition. So this is not a case of the critical editions on one side and the traditional text on the other — modern editors differ among themselves [C3].
significance.interpretation:
As Larry Herzog Jr. observes in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*, this is a benediction doubling one Paul has already given a few verses earlier, and its pastoral weight is essentially nil [C5]. That is the right size for it. The blessing is not in question: it stands at 16:20 in all seven editions on this list [C2]. What differs is whether the closing section of the letter gives it a second time.

The reason it is worth a note anyway is the company it keeps. The publishers report a disagreement among modern critical editions here, and that is more instructive than the verse itself. A reader who has learned to sort Bibles into two camps — old manuscripts against the traditional text — will find the sorting fails here. Editors weigh evidence and reach different judgments, and an edition is a set of decisions rather than a side in a dispute.

What cannot be said from this comparison is which way the doubling ran. That the same blessing appears twice is an observation; explaining how it came to appear twice requires evidence of a kind seven printed editions do not supply.

significance.sourceObservation:
Romans closes with a doxology — to the God who is able to strengthen you, to the only wise God be glory through Jesus Christ. Every edition compared here contains it. What they disagree about is where it belongs.

The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition and Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus print it at the very end, as 16:25–27 [S1, S2, S4, S5, S7]. The Majority Standard Bible and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text place it earlier, straight after 14:23, where it is numbered 14:24–26 [S3, S6, C2]. The doxology is present in all seven editions, but its position differs. There are also smaller wording differences; Nestle 1904 has an additional “of the ages” at the end of verse 27 compared with Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd.

This is a different kind of difference from most in this collection, and it is worth naming as such. Elsewhere the question is whether a sentence belongs in the text at all. Here it is a question of placement. BSB adds a footnote at 16:27 reporting that some manuscripts put the passage after Romans 14:23 or after Romans 15:33 [S1].
significance.interpretation:
This note concerns the doxology’s placement; smaller wording differences are a separate question. At the end of chapter 16 it closes the letter after the greetings. After 14:23 it comes before the continuation of Paul’s discussion of the weak and the strong in chapter 15, and the letter continues for two more chapters.

A reader is entitled to find that odd, and it is fair to say that a three-verse doxology sitting mid-letter reads strangely to most eyes. But strangeness is not evidence, and neither is familiarity. That the position most of us grew up with feels right is a fact about us, not about Paul's manuscript.

What a teacher can say is that the doxology is Scripture in both arrangements, that it is present in every edition compared here, and that where Paul placed it is a genuine question on which editions differ. What a teacher should not do is treat a placement difference as though the doxology were absent from one of these editions or offer an explanation of how the passage came to sit in two places, which would require evidence this comparison does not contain.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul lists what love's absence empties out: giving away everything, and then handing over his body — either *to be burned*, or *that I may boast*. The editions divide over which.

The Majority Standard Bible and Young's Literal Translation read "to be burned," and so do the Greek editions here: Nestle's 1904 text, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus, differing among themselves only over the verb's form [C1]. The Berean Standard Bible and the Berean Literal Bible instead render the boast: "exult in the surrender of my body," "that I may boast" [C2].

One thing about this comparison should be said openly. **No Greek edition displayed here carries the reading BSB and BLB translate** [C2]. BSB and MSB discuss the alternative readings in their footnotes, BSB reporting that the editions it names read "burned," MSB reporting that NA and WH read the boast [C3]. So at this verse the Greek you can see is not the Greek behind two of the English texts you can see — a limit of the comparison, not a fault in the translations.
significance.interpretation:
The difference is a single word, and in Greek the two are close: καυθήσωμαι and καυχήσωμαι differ by one letter in the middle. What they say is not close at all.

*That I may be burned* imagines martyrdom — the most extreme self-giving a reader could picture — and says that even that, without love, profits nothing. *That I may boast* imagines the opposite motive, and says that a surrender made for the sake of glory profits nothing either. The first reading measures love against the greatest sacrifice; the second measures it against the purest self-interest.

Paul's argument survives both, and it is the same argument: without love, the act gains the actor nothing. But the rhetorical shape shifts, and a preacher working from one reading will build a different paragraph than one working from the other. That is a real difference and it should not be smoothed away.

What cannot be settled here is which Paul wrote. Editors have divided, the English editions in this collection have divided with them, and no comparison of printed texts resolves it. A teacher can lay the two readings side by side, show that the point about love holds under either, and leave the question where the evidence leaves it.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul quotes what looks like an early hymn: great is the mystery of godliness — and then the first word of the hymn differs between editions.

Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus read Θεός: *God was manifested in the flesh*. Nestle's 1904 edition reads Ὃς: *who was manifested in the flesh* [C1]. The English editions follow. The Majority Standard Bible says "God appeared," and Young's Literal Translation says "God was manifested"; the Berean Standard Bible says "He appeared" and the Berean Literal Bible "[He] who appeared" [C2]. Both Berean editions footnote the alternative, and both keep that note separate from a second one about whether to render "vindicated by the Spirit" or "in spirit" [C3].

In the hand used by early Greek copyists, the two words are written very nearly alike. *God* was abbreviated as a sacred name, and the difference between the two forms comes down to a horizontal stroke through a letter and a line above it [C4]. That is a fact about how Greek was written, not a claim about what happened at this verse.
significance.interpretation:
A reader who finds "He appeared" where his memory says "God was manifest" may reasonably feel something has been taken away. It is worth answering that directly rather than hurrying past it.

Under either reading, the sentence declares the incarnation, and its subject is Christ. Under the Byzantine and TR reading it names him God outright. Under the critical reading the pronoun looks back to the mystery Paul has just announced and the hymn describes the same Person — appearing in flesh, vindicated by the Spirit, taken up in glory. No one reading this verse in any edition on the list could think the subject was anyone but Christ.

Larry Herzog Jr. describes the manuscript record for this word in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*. The account below is reported from his book; manuscript images and a critical apparatus have not been independently checked for this note. In Codex Sinaiticus the original scribe wrote ΟΣ — *who* — with no stroke and no overline; a first corrector left it as written, and a later corrector, working some centuries afterward, added the stroke through the omicron and the line above that make it ΘΣ, *God*. Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus show the same correction layer. On his account the early hands wrote *hos* and later correctors changed it to *theos*, while the reading with *God* is carried by the great mass of Byzantine manuscripts, by the printed Greek New Testament from Erasmus onward, and by the King James tradition [C7].

That is evidence about which reading is older. It is not evidence that anyone was tampering. A corrector who makes a devout reading explicit is doing something different from a forger, and the manuscripts preserve both layers side by side for anyone to examine — which is why the case can be described at all.

The doctrine is not carried by this word in any case. Lutherans confess with the whole church that the Son of God is true God, begotten of the Father from eternity, and true man born of the virgin Mary — the Nicene Creed's article on the Son, taken up in Augsburg Confession III [C5]. That confession rests on the whole witness of Scripture, and the same collection includes John 1:18, where the critical edition is the one calling the Son *God* and the traditional text says *Son* [C6]. Neither tradition is trying to raise or lower Christ.

Which word Paul wrote is a genuine question, and this comparison of printed editions does not settle it.

significance.sourceObservation:
Some Bibles read, at 1 John 5:7, that there are three that bear witness in heaven — the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit — and that these three are one; and then, at verse 8, that there are three that bear witness on earth. Others read only that there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water and the blood.

Of the seven editions compared here, **two** carry the longer reading. Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus prints it, and Young's Literal Translation prints it inside square brackets that open in verse 7 and close in verse 8 [C1, C2]. The other five — the Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Nestle's 1904 Greek edition and the Robinson–Pierpont Byzantine text — read the short form [C1].

That division is worth noting carefully. This is not the critical editions against the traditional text. **The Byzantine editions read the short form too.** Both Berean publishers attribute the longer reading to the Textus Receptus and to particular named editions, and neither attributes it to the Byzantine text [C3].
significance.interpretation:
The doctrine of the Trinity does not rest on this sentence, and it is worth saying so plainly to a reader meeting the difference for the first time.

Lutherans confess with the whole church one God in three persons, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, of one divine essence and power, co-eternal — the Nicene and Athanasian Creeds, and Augsburg Confession I [C4]. That confession was framed, taught and defended from the whole witness of Scripture. The wording difference at 1 John 5:7 does not by itself tell us an edition’s or a church’s confessional position.

The manuscript picture is set out by Larry Herzog Jr. in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*. The account below is reported from his book; manuscript readings and a critical apparatus have not been independently checked for this note. On his account Sinaiticus and Vaticanus from the fourth century and Alexandrinus from the fifth lack the Comma. Among the Greek copies he lists as containing it are Codex 629, which he dates to the fourteenth century, Codex Montfortianus (minuscule 61), which he dates to the early sixteenth, and later copies [C6].

That is a considerable body of evidence and it points one way. It is also not the whole of the story — the passage has a long history in the Latin west and a tangled one in the printed editions — and this short note does not attempt the whole of it.

What the longer reading does add, where it stands, is an unusually compact statement of the three persons in a single sentence. Losing it from the running text of an edition is a loss of that convenience, not of the doctrine.

What a teacher should resist is the two errors that meet here. One treats the shorter reading as an attack on the Trinity; it is not, and the Byzantine editions reading the short form are not suspected of any such thing. The other treats the longer reading as obviously spurious and its defenders as foolish; the question of what John wrote is a historical one, and this comparison of printed editions does not decide it.

title: Tree or Book: The Warning at the End of Revelation

καὶ ἐάν τις ἀφαιρῇ ἀπὸ τῶν λόγων βίβλου τῆς προφητείας ταύτης, ἀφαιρήσει ὁ Θεὸς τὸ μέρος αὐτοῦ ἀπὸ Βίβλου τῆς ζωῆς, καὶ ἐκ τῆς πόλεως τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν βιβλίῳ τούτῳ.

significance.sourceObservation:
Revelation closes with a warning against adding to or taking away from the words of the prophecy. This note considers two distinct differences among the editions inside that warning.

The first is a noun. Five of the seven editions name *the tree of life* — the Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Nestle's 1904 edition and Robinson–Pierpont. Boyd's Greek Textus Receptus reads *from the book of life*, and Young's Literal Translation reads "from the scroll of the life" [C1]. The Majority Standard Bible footnotes the Book of Life reading and attributes it to the Textus Receptus [C3].

The second is the mood of a verb. Nestle's edition and Boyd's Textus Receptus both state it flatly — God *will* take away. Robinson–Pierpont reads an optative: *may* God take away, a wish rather than a prediction. The Majority Standard Bible renders the wish and footnotes the other [C2, C3]. Both differences are in the Greek, not in English style.
significance.interpretation:
There is an irony in finding textual differences inside a warning about tampering with a text, and it is worth naming rather than tiptoeing around. But the warning is about adding to and taking from the prophecy — not about the ordinary work of copying, comparing and printing that stands behind every edition on your shelf. An editor deciding between two readings his manuscripts offer him is not the person John is warning.

What changes between the readings is real but bounded. "Tree of life" ties the loss to Revelation's own imagery, the tree in the city that appears a few verses earlier. "Book of life" ties it to the register of the redeemed named throughout the book. Both images are Revelation's; the question is which one John used here.

The verb makes a subtler difference. As a statement, the sentence announces what God will do. As a wish, it invokes it. Either way the sanction stands and its severity is unchanged.

What no one can determine from this comparison is which readings John wrote. A teacher can show both, note that five editions name the tree while Boyd and Young name the book or scroll, and leave the historical question where the evidence leaves it — including resisting the temptation to make the warning itself an argument about which edition to trust.

significance.sourceObservation:
Paul closes 2 Corinthians with a holy kiss, greetings from the saints, and the benediction naming Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Every edition here contains all of it. They divide it into verses differently.

Nestle's 1904 Greek edition prints the kiss and the greeting together as verse 12, and the benediction as verse 13 — so the letter ends at 13:13. The other six editions print three verses, ending at 13:14 [C1]. Both Berean editions footnote that texts vary in the numbering of these last verses [C3]. No words are added or dropped by this; the same sentences are grouped under different numbers.

A second and separate difference sits in the benediction itself. The Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus close with *Amen*. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible and Nestle's edition do not [C2]. That one is about a word rather than a number, and BSB and MSB report it in their notes about verse numbering [C3].
significance.interpretation:
Two lessons sit here, and the first is the more useful.

Verse numbers are a convenience laid over the text, not part of it. They were introduced in the sixteenth century, and a difference in sentence divisions can change the numbers without changing the words. If you look up 2 Corinthians 13:14 and your Bible stops at 13, nothing is missing. The benediction is there, numbered 13.

The second concerns the Amen. Liturgical endings attract an Amen, and the word appears at the close of many New Testament letters in some editions and not others. Whether Paul wrote it here is a real question and the editions differ; what a congregation says at the end of a benediction is a separate matter and is not settled by it.

Neither difference touches what the benediction says. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit are present in all seven editions, though the English renderings differ [C5] — which is worth noticing, since this is the verse from which the church's most familiar trinitarian blessing is drawn.

significance.sourceObservation:
Third John ends with the writer saying he hopes to come and speak face to face, followed by "Peace to you," greetings from the friends, and an instruction to greet the friends there by name.

Every edition compared here contains that closing material. The numbering difference concerns where verse 14 stops. Nestle's 1904 Greek edition ends verse 14 at "face to face" and makes the closing greetings verse 15, so the letter has fifteen verses. The Berean Standard Bible, the Berean Literal Bible, the Majority Standard Bible, Young's Literal Translation, Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd's Textus Receptus put the whole ending in verse 14, so the letter has fourteen [C1].

Both Berean editions note it in the same words: some translators begin a new verse 15 after "face to face" [C3]. The verse-numbering difference does not remove any of the closing material. There is also a small Greek word-order difference: Nestle places σε before ἰδεῖν, while Robinson–Pierpont and Boyd place it after. That is separate from how the verses are divided.
significance.interpretation:
The numbering difference itself changes no words. Editors divided the closing material differently; the separate Greek word-order difference does not account for the extra verse number.

That makes it useful, because it shows what verse numbers are. As Larry Herzog Jr. notes in *Ad Fontes – Volume One*, verse numbers were added to the New Testament in the sixteenth century, roughly fifteen hundred years after the letters were written [C5]. They serve the reader, not the text. Where a book is short and its closing runs on, editors have to decide whether the farewell is one unit or two — and reasonable editors have decided differently.

For a reader the practical consequence is small but worth knowing. If a commentary or a hymnal cites 3 John 15 and your Bible stops at 14, you have not lost a verse. Look at the end of verse 14 and you will find the words. The reverse also holds: a reference to the end of 3 John 14 may point at something your edition numbers 15.

Nothing about the letter's teaching, its greetings or its close depends on which way an editor divided them.
